description:
Health Copilot+ is an offline PWA for deep space (Moon/Mars) with signal delays up to 22m. Key features: 

1) Personal MAD Baselines over population averages

 2) Sensor Quality Gates to filter artifacts & false alarms

3) CUSUM analytics for slow biometric drift

 4) Radiation tracking with NASA-STD-3001 limits & Earth-analogs

 5) Delay-scaling autonomy with offline emergency checklists
summary:
HealthCopilot+ is an offline-first mission health console (NASA Space Apps prototype) that gives deep-space crews explainable, quality-aware health decision support when ground contact is unavailable. Instead of fixed thresholds, it checks signal quality first, uses each crew member's own median/MAD baseline, and shows the evidence behind every alert.

Problems solved: alarm fatigue from motion artifacts, the black-box explainability gap, communication latency on missions like a Mars transit, and baseline contamination from radiation spikes or sensor faults.

Workflow: (1) Sensor Collection of heart rate, SpO₂, CO₂ and radiation; (2) Quality Gating of motion artifacts and noise; (3) Personal Context via personal baselines; (4) Bounded Action, such as "re-seat sensor" or "queue ground review".

Features: Mission Overview, Alert Evidence Trail, Personal Rhythm (7/30/90-day trends), Crew Check-in (reported data kept separate from telemetry), Space & Cabin Lab (CO₂ and simulated Solar Particle Events), and a Scenario Simulator for fault injection.

Stack: React, TypeScript, Vite, Framer Motion, Tailwind CSS; a deterministic offline engine (no backend, no LLM); a Python pipeline (fetch_donki.py); a JSON rules engine linking alerts to sources; deployed on Vercel.

Data: NASA CCMC DONKI, NOAA SWPC, PhysioNet BIDMC, UCI WESAD.
details:
HealthCopilot+ is an offline-first mission health console that gives deep-space crews explainable, quality-aware health decision support when ground contact is delayed or unavailable. It works in four steps. First, it ingests deterministic telemetry: heart rate, SpO₂, CO₂ and radiation. Second, a quality gate detects motion artifacts and sensor noise before any alarm can fire. Third, each reading is compared with the crew member's own robust median/MAD baseline instead of a fixed population threshold. Fourth, the system suggests a bounded next step, such as "re-seat sensor" or "queue ground review". Every alert has an evidence trail showing raw values, baseline bands, quality scores and confidence. Reviewers can test the whole system in a Scenario Simulator by injecting faults, simulated Solar Particle Events and communication delays.

  • Fewer false alarms: In our seeded benchmark, false alerts dropped by 75% compared with fixed thresholds (1 versus 4), with 94% event detection sensitivity and 2.4 minutes average alert latency.
  • Explainability: Crews can see why an alert fired and which rule and source it came from, so they are not left guessing.
  • Autonomy: It runs locally with no backend and no LLM calls, so it keeps working when ground support is far away.
  • Cleaner baselines: Environmental events such as radiation spikes and sensor faults are identified and isolated, so they do not contaminate a crew member's baseline.

The goal is to make health monitoring on long-duration missions, such as a Mars transit, trustworthy enough for crews to act on without waiting for Mission Control. Fewer false alarms reduce alarm fatigue, so real alerts keep their weight. Visible evidence builds crew trust in the system. The approach is meant to show that physiological monitoring in deep space can be both rigorous and humane. It is a prototype and a research demonstration, not a clinical product.

  • Frontend: React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS and Framer Motion.
  • Logic and data: A seeded deterministic local engine, a JSON rules engine (engine/rules/) that links each alert to its source, and a Python pipeline (fetch_donki.py).
  • Project setup and hosting: pnpm workspace, GitHub and Vercel.
  • Data and APIs: NASA CCMC DONKI for solar event timing, NOAA SWPC for proton-flux profiles, and PhysioNet BIDMC and UCI WESAD for signal-noise and motion-artifact shape checks.

Most monitors ask "is this value too high?" HealthCopilot+ asks "can I trust this signal?" first. That "quality before alarm" ordering is the core idea. It also combines several things rarely seen together in one prototype:

  • Personal median/MAD baselines.
  • A per-alert evidence trail.
  • Bounded, human-readable actions.
  • A strict separation between crew-reported data and telemetry.
  • A reviewer-facing Scenario Simulator that lets judges break the system and watch how it responds.

The interface is deliberately calm and plain-language, so it supports crews under stress.

  • Signal quality: Motion artifacts, sensor noise and environmental events can all produce misleading readings.
  • Alarm fatigue: The aim is to reduce false positives without hiding real events.
  • Latency and connectivity: The system must work offline, with no dependence on a backend or an LLM.
  • Traceability: Every alert links to a rule and an external source in a source registry.
  • Honest scope: No real astronaut data is assumed or ingested, and results come from seeded benchmarks, not clinical validation.
  • Reviewability: Judges can try the live app and inject faults themselves.
